entries.title: Six Takeaways From the Commanders’ Roster Cuts
entries.summary: Julian Good-Jones, Shy Tuttle and Fabian Moreau are among the most surprising cuts of the weekend.
entries.content:
After weeks of training camp and three preseason games, the Commanders have whittled their roster down to 53 players. There were many players who didn’t see reps during practice or games who were likely to end up as final cuts. But a handful of players entered Friday’s preseason finale in tight position battles.

Here’s a look at some of the more surprising cuts, followed by a complete list of players released this weekend.

Center Julian Good-Jones

This wasn’t as much of a surprise as it was a well-known secret. The Commanders opened training camp with plans for Nick Allegretti to move into the starting center role, but those hopes were dashed early when Allegretti went down with an injury. Good-Jones took a majority of the reps in Allegretti’s absence, and it didn’t go well. On the first offensive possession of the Lions game, he missed a block that led to a pressure on Jayden Daniels. Rookie Matt Gulbin replaced him soon after, a sign of things to come.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Defensive tackle Byron Cowart

Since the first preseason game against the Dolphins on Aug. 14, it seemed like a two-way battle between Cowart and Ricky Barber for a backup spot on the defensive line. Barber, who was a member of the team’s practice squad last season, had one sack this preseason and tied for the team lead in tackles (14) and hits on the quarterback (3). While Cowart didn’t register a sack, he registered 10 tackles (two for loss) and two quarterback hits. Two of his pressures against Miami led to interceptions. In the end, Barber may have seemed more versatile at penetrating the line and defending the run.

Quarterback Sam Hartman

Hartman, a 2024 undrafted free agent, spent the past two seasons shuttling between the team’s practice squad and the active roster. He seemed destined for that fate again this season before rookie Athan Kaliakmanis took off in the preseason. Hartman (65% completion rate, 211 yards, 0 touchdowns) and Kaliakmanis (64.9%, 294 yards, 0 touchdowns) had similar numbers, but it was the rookie who showed a higher ceiling, particularly with long throws to Jaden Bradley and Nick Nash against Detroit.

Defensive tackle Shy Tuttle and cornerback Fabian Moreau

Moreau and Tuttle are the biggest surprises on this list. Tuttle stepped in because of injuries to Daron Payne and Tim Settle, and he has performed pretty well this summer. Moreau was one of the 41 players who sat out the preseason finale against the Ravens on Friday, which normally signals a player is safe. But their inclusion in this list could very well be a technicality: A team source said both will probably be re-signed Monday after the team moves left tackle Laremy Tunsil and defensive tackle Jer’Zhan Newton to injured reserve.

Offensive lineman Max Scharping

Scharping’s release means guard Tanoa Togiai is the biggest winner on the offensive line. The undrafted free agent from Utah didn’t generate much buzz out of camp until the final week. As of now, the 6-foot-6 Togiai is the only backup guard on the roster.

Wide receiver Van Jefferson

Jefferson was a casualty of the roster crunch created by Stefon Diggs’ arrival. The seven-year veteran was one of the more consistent players through camp, getting shout-outs from coach Dan Quinn on multiple occasions. But once Diggs was signed Aug. 7, Jefferson became expendable. Two of the team’s seven receiver spots were taken by returners Jaylin Lane and Luke McCaffrey, which left Jefferson battling Dyami Brown and Treylon Burks for reps.

entries.title: Election Officials Brace for Chaos Over Trump's Mail-in Ballot Rule
entries.summary: “If the system fails, North Carolina may be unable to mail ballots to voters at all,” a state official said.
entries.content:
Election officials in nearly half the states are warning the courts that implementing the U.S. Postal Service’s new mail ballot rule would cause significant turmoil in their plans for the midterm elections, with plenty of signs voters would lose their chance to vote.

In declarations filed in a lawsuit seeking to halt the ballot rule, the officials detail how the rule comes late in the process, squeezes deadlines for sending out ballots and clashes with long-standing state election laws and carefully timed procedures.

“It is currently less than a week from when we need to provide our mailing list to our print and mail vendor,” said Sarah Hanzas, the secretary of state in Vermont, where there is universal vote-by-mail. “My staff, the city and town clerks, and the vendor have not seen or been trained on the new USPS system. We are not alone in this lack of knowledge.”

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Massachusetts temporarily blocked the executive order late Thursday for 14 days, a decision the Trump administration has appealed.

North Carolina is supposed to begin sending out ballots Friday. Marc Brunton, an assistant deputy attorney general, was among the election officials who pointed out the rule would require jurisdictions to submit envelope designs to USPS and receive feedback.

“Given the very short time available and the untested technology that the Rule relies on, I have profound concerns that the Rule will prevent eligible voters from voting, including in the November 2026 general election,” Brunton said in the court filings.

States will have to upload the name and address of every eligible voter, as well as a unique “Intelligent Mail” barcode to the USPS Ballot Portal — a system that election staff will need to be trained to use. And they won’t be able to enroll voters in bulk.

“Elections officials will not only be required to process these mailings within their own systems, but they will bear the added burden of processing mailings in an entirely new system operated by USPS — about which officials currently have no concrete operational information,” Brunton said. “If the system fails, North Carolina may be unable to mail ballots to voters at all.”

Alongside the privacy concerns associated with sending out voter information, intelligence mail barcodes cost money, especially at the scale that states require.

These are all steps, election officials say, that will be costly and timely. Several states have already ordered ballots that do not comply with the executive order. Others have never used intelligent mail barcodes.

In Hawaii, the chief election officer pointed out the kind of unique logistical challenges facing election officials.

“The new USPS rule would require us to throw out the previously ordered size 10 envelopes, at a cost of over $79,000.00, as they were already printed with a static Intelligent Mail Barcode for each county clerk,” Scott Nago said in a declaration. “It may not be possible to get new orders of size 10 envelopes delivered to Hawaii from the continent on such short notice.”

Delays are another concern — one that has plagued previous elections. Whether states accept mail-in ballots after Election Day or not, some have already complained about the delays in election mail prior to the USPS taking on the responsibility of sorting through which citizens are or are not eligible.

USPS has also said it does not plan “to require additional staff” to take on this responsibility.

Mandy Vigil, state election director in New Mexico, was among the officials who pointed out that voter lists will continue to change ahead of Election Day, with new registrations, current registrations being modified or existing registrations canceled for people moving or dying.

“As such, any ‘point-in-time’ eligible list provided by the federal government agencies will not match New Mexico’s dynamic voter list,” Vigil said. “Having inconsistent eligible voter lists will cause confusion, disenfranchise large numbers of New Mexico voters, and create chaos for the election administrators.”

Nevada’s deputy secretary of state, Mark Wlaschin, highlighted a part of the final rule from the USPS that says the data collection will be used to enable “law enforcement to better detect potential issues meriting further investigation,” an unprecedented tactic that he says could make voters wary.

“The threat of disclosing such information to law enforcement officials itself could suppress voter participation,” Wlaschin said in a declaration. “And each of the process changes create delay and administrative burden at each step, creating dangerous bottlenecks in the short time before elections that increase the risks of cascading impacts and disenfranchisement at an alarming scale.”

Advocates worry that the sheer confusion behind these wavering court decisions, or the potential implementation of the final rule with the court’s permission, could confuse already vulnerable voters. Nearly one-third of Americans voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election.

Joanna Southard, assistant chief of California’s Elections Division, was among other officials who said in the declarations that access to mail-in voting is especially important for rural and disabled voters. States mail ballots to eligible, active registered voters who are out of the state on Election Day because they are in college, traveling or in the military.

Southard said that of the 9.4 million people who voted in the state’s primary this year, 89% of them voted by mail. The sheer capacity of the changes such a large state would have to make could debilitate eligible voters.

“That Rule is causing and will imminently cause significant harm, confusion, and disruption in California’s election administration, and will impose unrecoverable costs on California,” Southard wrote.

Later, she added, “Even if USPS’s untested Ballot Portal works as intended and does not experience technical problems — which seems unlikely given the short development and implementation window — enrolling all 23 million voters with USPS will be a massive undertaking.”

entries.title: The Push Toward At-Home Care Is Caught in Trump’s Anti-Fraud Crusade
entries.summary: The Trump administration is holding more money from California’s home-care program than anywhere else.
entries.content:
Thousands of Californians unable to feed, bathe and dress themselves have struggled to find caregivers, prompting the state to swell its in-home care program.

That effort is now being thrown back in its face.

The Trump administration is citing the rapid growth of California’s in-home services as evidence of fraud, withholding more money from it than any other single health program in the country.

The administration has paused $2.2 billion in Medicaid funds to the state, most of that — $1.7 billion — for California’s In-Home Supportive Services, putting the program at risk for cuts. The funds are being held as part of the administration’s high-profile crusade against fraud in federal safety net programs, led by Vice President JD Vance.

California officials say there’s no evidence the state’s personal-care program, among the nation’s most generous, has especially high levels of fraud. They fear the Trump administration is undermining the community-based approach Democrats and Republicans have supported for decades.

“If CMS is able to point out strong or major fraud concerns, we’d be happy to know about it,” said California Medicaid Director Tyler Sadwith. “Unfortunately, they haven't done that.”

California’s expansion effort began in 2021 when the state’s auditor identified a crucial flaw in the program that pays family members and caregivers to assist more than 900,000 disabled and elderly Californians with their daily personal care.

“You feel stuck,” Ligia Andrade Zúñiga, a 47-year-old disabled San Mateo resident, told NOTUS of life without a caregiver. “The four walls of your room become like a jail.”

A 2009 car accident paralyzed Zúñiga from the chest down. Since then, she has struggled for years at a time to find a consistent caregiver. She didn’t like asking her elderly mother to help her get out of bed, use the bathroom, brush her teeth and eat breakfast — but sometimes she had to. It strained their relationship, and she felt isolated, depressed and fought thoughts of self-harm.

“One of the biggest issues in this space over the past 10 years has been lack of caregivers and not sufficient services to meet demand,” Damon Terzaghi, vice president for Medicaid and home care policy at the National Alliance for Care at Home, a membership organization that represents providers.

But to Vance’s anti-fraud task force — which has deferred unprecedented sums of Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota this year — California’s expansion appears nefarious.

Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, told reporters in July that spending on in-home programs went up by 24% in California over the last two fiscal years, compared with 12% on average for the rest of the country.

California says it’s complying with CMS’s requests for more information as the agency evaluates its funding in a process that could take months or more to work through. CMS did not respond to requests for comment.

The anti-fraud task force has dialed up the government’s focus on scams and deceit to previously unseen levels. Vance has regularly issued dire threats against scammers who officials say have been bilking the nation’s safety net programs unchecked for years.

Everyone agrees there’s some degree of fraud in entitlement programs. States have always worked on prosecuting it, some more earnestly than others. And personal-care providers have indeed been convicted of Medicaid fraud at higher rates nationally than other types of health care workers.

Yet the administration’s anti-fraud work has taken a sharp political tack. So far, it has held up large sums only from California and Minnesota — but not Florida, home to many massive fraud schemes. Nor has it provided specific evidence for withholding so much from California’s home-care program, merely citing faster growth in California’s program compared to other states, as well as “statistical anomalies” in the state’s data.

Vance and other Cabinet members in the task force trumpet their largely blue-state-focused efforts ahead of the midterm elections, insisting prosecution has been insufficient and promising to root out fraud once and for all.
JD Vance (5441x3671, AR: 1.48)“We’ve got a party that is fighting for fraud, and a party that is fighting against fraud,” Vance told an audience in Milwaukee in early July. “When you come to vote in November, are you going to vote for the pro-fraud party?”

While it’s normal for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to temporarily pause some Medicaid payments to states to double-check receipts, administrations have never deferred so much money for entire categories of services, experts say.

Public health administrators are also taken aback by the administration’s targeting of home health services, fearing the Trump administration is undermining policies federal and state lawmakers have prioritized for nearly 50 years.

Former President Ronald Reagan signed a law in 1981 that pushed people from institutional care to home services, as the public health community settled on home care as the more humane and less expensive approach. In 1999, the Supreme Court found that unnecessarily institutionalizing people with disabilities is illegal discrimination under the Americans with Disabilities Act. The federal government has long interpreted that decision as requiring states to offer home- and community-based services in most cases.

Now, the Trump administration is reconsidering that legal mandate.

Earlier this summer, the Justice Department said it won’t enforce its own guidance implementing that Supreme Court decision as it writes new guidelines. It also released a memo calling into question how that decision about not institutionalizing people with disabilities has been interpreted for decades.

Oz has also repeatedly questioned whether the government should pay family members to care for loved ones at home.

“Personal care services: these help Medicaid patients do something that our families would normally do for us, like carrying groceries,” Oz said in a social media video in March about a CMS probe focused on New York, adding that the program is being abused.

He acknowledged at a July press conference that “done correctly, these programs could make sense.”

Hagar Dickman, an advocate for long-term services in California at the nonprofit Justice in Aging, said Oz’s comments show a misunderstanding of how personal care works. In most cases, to be eligible for In-Home Supportive Services, a patient must require around-the-clock care beyond what a typical family member with a full-time job could offer.

“The most generous interpretation of that statement is that it’s out of touch with what Americans and what Californians need financially in order to be secure in their homes,” Dickman said. “Most Californians require a two-income household.”

For the first 15 years of Amanda Andresen’s life, her mother, Rosa, didn’t know she could get paid for caring for her. Amanda’s brain lacks a critical bridge of fibers separating its left and right halves. She is 28 years old but cognitively around 15 months old.

Rosa is constantly by Amanda’s side. She keeps Amanda safe during daily seizures. She changes her diapers. She shreds Amanda’s chicken into tiny pieces that she’s able to swallow. She keeps Amanda from wandering away in the grocery store.
IMG_0459 copy.jpg (6145x4032, AR: 1.52)“From the moment she gets up, I have to help her,” Rosa told NOTUS.

After Rosa’s husband died in 2013, leaving her without income, she learned she could qualify to be paid $19.65 an hour under IHSS.

She applied, submitted to a background check and attended training. A social worker visited her home to determine how many hours of paid care Amanda qualified for. At first, Amanda was granted just two hours a day, but after Rosa appealed the decision, it was upped to roughly nine hours a day — the maximum a patient can get.

Now Rosa brings in around $5,560 a month plus smaller supplemental security income checks — enough to pay their $2,700 rent and cover living expenses with help from food stamps. To get paid, she enters her hours in an online portal. She can’t work more than 283 hours a month.

That’s unquestionably cheaper than keeping a patient in a 24-hour facility. IHSS costs Medi-Cal roughly $17,000 a year per recipient, compared to well over $100,000 for a skilled nursing facility, according to 2021 estimates by the state auditor.

“This model has been universally accepted across parties for such a long time as the most cost-effective way of providing care,” said Arnulfo De La Cruz, president of SEIU Local 2015, which represents home health workers.

Some personal-care assistants do commit fraud. States convicted far more personal-care providers last year — 326 in total — than any other type of caregiver, the Department of Health and Human Services Inspector General found. (That figure may also be influenced by the type of cases prosecutors typically pursue.)

Home health care claims were a significant part of a massive batch of prosecutions the anti-fraud task force announced in June. Nearly half of the state cases involved personal-care assistants. Missouri had the most.

In one case, St. Louis resident Patricia Busby billed Medicaid $18,278 for services she claimed to have provided to her adult daughter Christine Busby — even as both women worked as armed security guards for three- to 12-hour shifts.

Four of the cases were in California, and they all involved individuals submitting false time sheets.
Vance Fraud Task Force (4323x2882, AR: 1.50)Yet at times the administration has tripped up in its eagerness to claim fraud. A month after Oz accused New York of turning its home-care program into a “massive jobs program,” the administration admitted it had inaccurately claimed that nearly three-fourths of the state’s Medicaid enrollees use personal-care services. CMS had misidentified the state’s billing codes in its analyses.

Some IHSS advocates and patients worry the intense scrutiny on personal care — on top of legislation passed last year by congressional Republicans projected to reduce Medicaid spending by hundreds of billions — could make the program eligible for future cuts in California and beyond.

The impact could be immense: Medicaid funds well over half of all home care in the United States, according to KFF.

States must offer certain services in Medicaid, but personal care is optional, making it an easy target for reductions. Cuts have recently been on the table in California. Gov. Gavin Newsom’s budget proposal released earlier this year included millions of dollars worth of cuts to IHSS, drawing sharp pushback from the disability community before the reductions were ultimately rejected.

The state, like others, has already installed checks meant to prevent fraudsters from siphoning off taxpayer dollars, including unannounced home visits and data checks meant to catch bad actors. Providers have to log their work in a GPS-enabled electronic time sheet, as required by Congress in 2016.

Keeping fraudsters out of the program and eligible people who need assistance in it is a delicate balance, said Alice Burns, associate director of KFF’s Program on Medicaid and the Uninsured. Take guardrails away, and both eligible patients and bad actors may benefit. Add too many hurdles meant to trip up fraudsters, and enrollees may have a difficult time accessing care — a problem California and many other states have already faced.

Access to caregivers can be life altering. Zúñiga said she has a good rapport with her current caregiver, who arrives early in the morning to help her get ready for work; she runs a disability rights nonprofit, serves on a local governance board for in-home services and is on her local school board.

“I cannot serve my community,” she said, “without being able to get up out of my bed in the morning.”

entries.title: Prime Real Estate
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Aug. 31, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Amazon wants to do it all. The tech giant is at once an online shopping mall, a streaming service, a cloud computing business, a grocer, a pharmacist and now … a local landlord?

Arlington Community High School, an alternative high school for county residents age 16 and over, opened a 30,000-square-foot campus across two floors of Amazon’s Arlington headquarters on Friday.

NOTUS reporter Zara Norman’s experience at the grand opening started the way many Amazon deliveries end up: late and at the wrong address. Eventually, the event got on its way next door to the school (which has a separate entrance) in a cavernous auditorium where parents and educators mingled with Amazon employees, snacked on sliders, sipped on smoothies, sat through a DJ set blasting censored pop hits and heard from local officials and tech executives on the nature of this unique partnership.

“We’re really just a facilities partner and obviously a community partner, and then Arlington Public Schools runs all the school and educational programming,” Andrea Fava, Amazon’s vice president of U.S. public policy, told NOTUS.

Amazon employees will do “a lot of volunteer events” at the school, a spokesperson told NOTUS, but Fava said the tech giant isn’t trying to move into education. Rather, the partnership is part of the company’s efforts to be a good community partner. Amazon also increased Arlington’s affordable housing stock by 23% as part of that commitment, with a $1.3 billion investment.

Though a speaker at Friday’s event graduated from ACHS last year and now works at Amazon, Fava told NOTUS that the company isn’t running any kind of employment scheme. She was “sure,” however, that there’d be “organic opportunities” for employment with the company.

School officials spoke glowingly of the partnership, which has allowed ACHS to find a permanent home at no cost after decades without a dedicated campus. The school signed a 30-year lease through which it gets the space for no cost other than those for routine maintenance and repairs (estimated at $25,000 per year, according to ARLNow).

“This new permanent home represents much more than a new space,” Francisco Durán, superintendent of Arlington Public Schools, said in a speech. “It represents opportunity, belonging and our community’s commitment to helping every student succeed. We are incredibly grateful to Amazon for its partnership and investment.”





DEEP DIVE

Tensions continue to rise at East Potomac Park. Cyclists, anglers, joggers and bird-watchers showed up to a rally at the island park Saturday ahead of President Donald Trump’s proposed start date on Tuesday for the construction of a new golf course.

With plenty of uncertainty still surrounding plans for the course and the widespread effect the changes could have on nearby recreational areas, protestors highlighted all the activities and communities that could be at stake. NOTUS’ Shamira Muhammad spoke to one cyclist who rode 30 miles down from Montgomery County to join the rally.

“When I got here, I saw people on their bikes, running, walking,” she said. “We should be encouraging that instead of taking away safe places where people can do it.”

The event occurred after days of tree removal across the island raised alarm. In a statement, the Interior Department called the work “routine maintenance” to remove “hazard trees.” But Saturday’s attendees were not convinced.

“[This is] the beginning of them tearing this entire space out,” one said, “and building it to be something that is not for the public.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

March on Washington AP - 26240709536451 (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)
Thousands gathered in front of the Lincoln Memorial on Friday for the 63rd anniversary of the March on Washington, with this year’s event centered on “defending the vote.” National leaders, including Al Sharpton, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Martin Luther King III, spoke out against red-state redistricting efforts and what they see as threats against voting rights.

Local leaders used the event as an opportunity to elevate the District’s fight for statehood. At-Large council member Robert White said the country has to “end second-class citizenship in the capital of the United States.” Janeese Lewis George highlighted the region’s inability to push for change without a vote in Congress. “This isn’t an oversight, my people,” she said. “This is disenfranchisement.”

Patients spend more time in the emergency department in D.C. than anywhere else in the country, Axios D.C. reports. Limited access to urgent and preventive care has pushed the average waiting time here to more than five hours, nearly twice the nationwide median. In the first year the city’s newest hospital, Cedar Hill, was in operation, about 80% of its more than 45,000 emergency room visits were for “low-acuity” conditions that could have been handled at urgent care, the hospital said.

The National Park Service released a report Friday in support of Trump’s proposed arch, though the agency acknowledged the adverse effects it could have on the District’s most iconic memorials and landmarks, NOTUS’ Marissa Martinez reports.

A federal grand jury indicted Melissa Farris, who live-streamed herself vandalizing D.C.’s World War II Memorial earlier this month, on Friday, City Cast D.C. reports.

Have you ever fired off an angry tweet to Metro, complaining of a late bus or sweltering train car? The Washington Post profiled the 11-person team tasked with responding in real time to hundreds of such comments per week, with a goal to reply to each within 15 minutes.





FROM MARYLAND

State regulators approved less than half of the rate increase Pepco requested, meaning the average resident will see an increase of about $3.94 a month instead of the proposed $10.24, WUSA9 reports.





D.C. TRIVIA


Which U.S. president was once arrested for speeding through D.C. on his horse and carriage?

  1. Abraham Lincoln
  2. Ulysses S. Grant
  3. Rutherford B. Hayes
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout-out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

The Commanders are one step closer to the regular season after trimming their roster to 53 players this weekend. In his breakdown of the moves, NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports that — to the surprise of no one — the offensive line remains the team’s biggest question mark.

The Spirit earned a much-needed win over Bay FC on Sunday, the team’s first victory in more than a month. NOTUS’ Alex Schiffer reports that the win ends a four-game slide that saw Washington post three losses and a tie, and keeps the Spirit in second place in the NWSL.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Marlins, 6:45 p.m. (FS1)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo by Francis Chung/Politico/AP.

entries.title: Double Duty
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Donald Trump, president/press secretary? Pentagon squares off with the press. Anti-fraud efforts may impede Californians’ health care. And: Election officials are concerned about the USPS rule. 

THE LATEST

A secretary of state who is also national security adviser and, for a time, the acting archivist of the United States and the acting administrator of USAID. A transportation secretary who doubled as NASA administrator. The head of the Office of Management and Budget who serves as senior adviser at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. A vice president/RNC finance chairman in one. And a treasury secretary who ran the IRS too for a while.

But no press secretary. 

Karoline Leavitt has departed her White House role but Donald Trump has yet to name her successor, and it’s not clear whom he favors. In the interim, the president may tap a rotating cast of Cabinet officials to take turns sparring with the press. (Meme-making Marco Rubio, for one, delighted in his time at the lectern.)

It’s been a theme in Trump 2.0 for his top officials to take on multiple roles, a move that has some worrying they may be over-tasked.

“Relying regularly on senior officials to serve in two, three and sometimes even four important roles simultaneously is yet another example of this administration embracing poor management,” Max Stier, the president and CEO of the Partnership for Public Service, told us.

“It's common sense that fielding a full team rather than requiring players to try to juggle multiple roles leads to better results,” Stier added. “But the stakes are much higher when we are talking about leading our government, and Americans will suffer further because of this governance malpractice.”

Trump also prefers to speak for himself, repeatedly making some of his administration's biggest announcements on his personal Truth Social account. And it looks like he could be even more accessible in the run-up to the midterms. Fox News' Peter Doocy reports that Trump may hold daily rallies in October, which would probably make news more often than a White House press briefing anyway.

Open tabs: Inside Trump’s Plan to Give the Pentagon a Stake in Venezuela’s Oil Riches (WSJ); USDA cyclospora research projects shelved amid funding cuts and relocations (Politico); Google Maps Changes Lake Ontario to Lake America (NYT)

From the Pentagon

Pete Derangement Syndrome: “It’s TDS and PDS — they hate President Trump and Secretary Hegseth more than they love America,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell posted on X yesterday, apparently referencing Trump Derangement Syndrome and what we assume is Pete Derangement Syndrome after his boss, Pete Hegseth.

Hegseth’s only job, he said Friday, is to Make the Department of War Great Again, and not run for president, as NBC had reported earlier that day he was considering, sparking Hegseth’s fury and a weekend of battling the press. Parnell took on The Washington Post yesterday for reporting that Pentagon brass warned that a sustained, large-scale military operation against Iran is unsustainable and risks America’s ability to confront threats across the globe and at home. As NOTUS’ Joe Gould writes, Parnell said the media “hate President Trump and Secretary Hegseth more than they love America.”

Seeking to combat that, Hegseth has installed his own influencer army with large online followings in government roles, the Post also reported yesterday, a team paid by taxpayers to amplify and defend Hegseth and Trump.

Friday also marked six months of America’s war against Iran, one that has had its starts and stops, its very own Versailles peace agreement, a closed-but-open Strait of Hormuz and, so far, 18 U.S. service member deaths and more than 750 injuries. After more than a week without fighting, the U.S. struck Iranian rocket launchers near the strait yesterday. Iran retaliated with its own strikes.

THE BIG ONE

Health care in limbo: Thousands of Californians unable to feed, bathe and dress themselves have struggled for years to find caregivers, leading the state to grow its in-home care program. But as the Trump administration ramps up its anti-fraud crusade, it’s targeting the program’s fast growth as evidence of fraud, NOTUS’ Paige Winfield Cunningham and Natalie Alms report. The feds have paused over $2 billion in Medicaid funds, leaving the future of a key program in the balance.

California officials told Paige and Natalie that the administration has been unable to point the state toward evidence of fraud in the program, and that they’re working to provide CMS the information it has requested. The funding pause is political, the California officials say, making an issue out of a program that has traditionally been prioritized by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

“If CMS is able to point out strong or major fraud concerns, we’d be happy to know about it,” California Medicaid Director Tyler Sadwith told our team. “Unfortunately, they haven't done that.”

NOTUS METRO


Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

After a Much-Needed Win, the Spirit Hopes to Regain Momentum, by Alex Schiffer

NEW ON NOTUS

Problems predicted: Election officials in nearly half of the states say in declarations in federal court that implementing the U.S. Postal Service’s new mail ballot rule would cause significant turmoil in their plans for the midterm elections, with plenty of signs that voters would lose their chance to vote. NOTUS’ Adora Brown sorted through the warnings as election officials ready ballots for the midterms.

“Given the very short time available and the untested technology that the Rule relies on, I have profound concerns that the Rule will prevent eligible voters from voting, including in the November 2026 general election,” North Carolina Assistant Deputy Attorney General Marc Brunton said in the court filings.

North Carolina, by the way, is slated to start mailing out ballots this Friday.

entries.title: At East Potomac Park, Trees Are Falling and Tensions Are Rising
entries.summary: On Saturday afternoon, a spirited protest was held not far from a tree-removal operation.
entries.content:
Cyclists, anglers, joggers and bird-watchers showed up to East Potomac Park on Saturday, hoping to bring awareness to the island’s uncertain future ahead of President Donald Trump’s proposed start date on Tuesday for construction of a new golf course.

Wearing shirts with slogans like “Save Hains Point” and holding signs with phrases such as “Fore the People, Not the President,” dozens of people represented the activities — and communities — that could be at stake if Trump’s plans move forward.

The rally was organized by the Washington Area Bicycle Association and Save East Po, a grassroots coalition aimed at protecting the area. It took place at the park’s southernmost tip, not far from where a tree-removal crew was working Saturday. At least six trees around the golf course were removed by National Park Service employees. Several dozen others had been taken out in the days before the rally, alarming activists and preservationists

The Interior Department, which oversees the National Park Service, said in a statement that arborists are doing routine maintenance, “with selective removal of hazard trees, non-native invasive trees, and declining and dying trees that cannot be brought back to good health through any degree of intervention.”

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

But WABA Executive Director Elizabeth Kiker said she’s concerned that the three-day removal operation was “the beginning of them tearing this entire space out and building it to be something that is not for the public.”

Kiker said she and some other attendees watched a few of the trees being cut down.

“Maybe they were ailing, but boy they sure didn't look like it,” she said.

There is still uncertainty about what will happen Tuesday, the date Trump highlighted in June as the start of construction. A lawsuit against the plans is currently at a standstill and, according to court documents, the government has not shared construction plans for the golf course, nor has it provided maps of trees slated for removal.

Save East Po founder Alex Rosen, who cycles, runs and golfs at East Potomac Park, said the lack of transparency has him concerned about the future of a beloved landmark.

“I sit on picnic benches at the very tip [of the park], just away from the hustle and bustle of downtown D.C.,” he told NOTUS. “I call my mom while I watch planes take off.”

East Potomac Tree Cutting NPS (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)
When he heard of plans for a proposed takeover of the golf course, he felt moved to do something. Rosen began tweeting any information he could find about the future of the park, but substantial updates have been hard to come by.

“We want to see the trees that they're planning on cutting down — they won't release that,” he said. “There's renderings of what the future golf course is going to look like, but they won't release that. There's clearly plans that exist right now, but this administration is acting without any semblance of transparency, and that's the problem.”

Rosen was joined at Saturday’s rally by outdoor enthusiasts of all stripes. Bird-watcher Summer Delehanty said East Potomac is one of favorite places to engage with her community.

“We [once] had a fork-tailed flycatcher, which is like a South American bird, show up,” she told NOTUS. “It actually landed in one of the trees that I know was just cut down.”

East Potomac Tree Cutting Saw (4227x2817, AR: 1.50)
Bob Hartt, a protestor from Alexandria who is legally blind, said he often rides a tandem bike through East Potomac Park with a captain, who calls out directions and upcoming turns. He said it’s one of the safest areas in the region where he’s able to do this.

“For people who are blind, if you're learning to ride on a bicycle, you can stop and start and practice without the fear of the real heavy traffic you get in other areas,” he said.

Theresa Furnari, who has been cycling in East Potomac Park since childhood, rode 30 miles from Montgomery County to protest. She said she’s afraid the public will lose access to the park, which has unobscured views of the Washington Monument, the Wharf and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

“When I got here, I saw people on their bikes, running, walking,” she said. “That's all really healthy activities, and we should be encouraging that instead of taking away safe places where people can do it.”

entries.title: D.C. Police Officer Dies After Shooting at Station
entries.summary: City officials say no one else was involved in the incident.
entries.content:
A police officer died early Monday morning after a shooting at the Second District station in Northwest D.C., though city officials say there was no one else involved in the incident.

“On Monday, August 31, 2026, at approximately 5:02 a.m., a [Metropolitan Police Department] officer suffered a critical injury from a gunshot wound while inside the Second District police station in the 3300 block of Idaho Avenue NW. The officer was transported to a nearby hospital, where they later succumbed to their injuries,” said an MPD spokesman in an email.

“MPD’s Internal Affairs Bureau responded to the scene to investigate. Nothing currently indicates that another party was involved,” they added.

The death comes almost two years to the date after investigator Wayne David died on August 28, 2024, after a gun he was trying to recover from a storm drain discharged.

Six MPD officers have died in the line of duty since 2000. The most recent came in January, when Officer Terry Bennett was struck and killed by a driver while assisting another motorist on I-695.

This story will be updated.
